title: 9.7 Binomial Distributions

icans: I can make and read a probability distribution.
I can tell when an experiment is binomial.
I can find binomial probabilities and interpret a binomial distribution.

vocab: a variable whose value is _____________ by the outcome of an experiment
a table, graph, or rule that gives the probability of each value of a random ___________; the probabilities add to 1
n ______________ trials, each with two outcomes (success or failure), and the same probability p of success each time

blocks.p: List all 16 outcomes of flipping 4 coins (HHHH, HHHT, …). Sort them by the number of heads.
Make a histogram of the probabilities on the back. Which number of heads is most likely? Why?

blocks.sec: Part 2 · Notes and examples (fill in each note, then work the example)

notes: Probability distribution: In a probability distribution, the probabilities add to ______.

blocks.stem: A bag has 3 balls labeled 1, 2 balls labeled 2, and 1 ball labeled 3. Let x be the number on a ball chosen at random. Make the probability distribution.
The histogram shows the distribution of x, the number of heads in 3 coin flips. What is the probability of getting at least 2 heads?

notes: Binomial experiment: A binomial experiment has n _______________ trials, each with ______ outcomes and the same probability p.
Fair coin: For a fair coin: P(k heads in n flips) = _______________ ÷ _______________

blocks.stem: You flip a coin 10 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 7 heads?
At a school, 70% of the students ride the bus. You choose 5 students at random. What is the probability that exactly 3 of them ride the bus?
You flip 6 coins. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
A basketball player makes 80% of her free throws. She shoots 4. Find the probability that she makes all 4, and the probability that she makes exactly 3.

tickets.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3, 4. What is P(x is even)?
You flip 4 coins. What is the probability of getting exactly 4 heads?
You guess on 3 multiple-choice questions, each with a 1/4 chance of being right. What is the probability of getting exactly 1 right?
